title: Ask useful questions before welcoming a chef home
intro: Private chef background checks in Dubai are part of a broader conversation about suitability. Clients also need to understand relevant cooking experience, communication and the practical fit with their home. This page helps you frame questions around the actual work being proposed. It explains why documentation, references, an introduction and a clear first menu serve different purposes, and why ongoing feedback still matters after the initial match. If you have an essential requirement, raise it before confirming the arrangement so it can be addressed directly.

sections.title: Connect every question to a real household need
paragraphs: If discretion is a priority, discuss household boundaries and communication. If you need a particular cuisine, ask about relevant cooking experience. If meals will be prepared for later, explore how the proposed chef would organise that work in your kitchen.

This makes the assessment more useful than asking only whether a chef is experienced. It also gives myCHEF a clearer basis for recommending a suitable professional. Any specific documents or assurances you require should be discussed through the booking process; a general description of checks should not replace that conversation.

sections.title: Ask about checks that relate to the proposed work
paragraphs: When assessing a chef service, ask questions that help you understand the person and arrangement being proposed. Relevant cooking experience, identity and work eligibility, references and food handling awareness all serve different purposes. A profile description alone does not answer every question about suitability for your household.

Discuss how practical ability is considered alongside documentation. You may want experience with a particular cuisine, confidence in a domestic kitchen or an organised approach to recurring preparation. The best evidence is connected to those needs, rather than a long list of credentials that may have little bearing on the work you are booking.

If a requirement is essential, raise it before confirming the match. Ask what information can be shared and how a specific concern will be addressed. Checks support an informed decision, but they do not remove the need for a clear brief, suitable kitchen conditions and ongoing feedback. A thoughtful introduction brings those parts together before the service begins.

sections.title: Look for a chef whose strengths fit the brief
paragraphs: A chef who excels at an elaborate tasting menu may not be the best match for a household that wants simple daily meals and careful batch preparation. Start with the work you actually need: particular cuisines, family cooking, confident service for guests or a regular routine with multiple meals. Relevant experience matters more than a list of impressive-sounding dishes.

Discuss the proposed chef's approach to your kitchen and schedule. How would the menu fit the available hours? Which dishes work well for later meals? What information would they need before the first visit? These practical questions make an introduction more useful than a general conversation about favourite food.

myCHEF considers the brief alongside availability when recommending a match. Profiles can help you understand cooking interests and service styles, but the proposed arrangement still needs confirmation. If you would like a paid trial or tasting, agree the purpose, menu and price first so you know exactly what you will be assessing.

sections.title: Set expectations for discretion in your home
paragraphs: Inviting a chef into your home involves more than sharing a kitchen. Explain any household boundaries before the visit: rooms that are private, preferred routes through the property and how to communicate while you are working or entertaining. Practical instructions make it easier for the service to fit naturally into your day.

Photography should be discussed separately from cooking. If your household does not want photographs taken, say so clearly in the brief. Any request to share images of a booking should be handled with the relevant permission; a meal at home is not automatically a marketing opportunity. You can also raise any specific confidentiality requirements before confirming the arrangement.

Keep sensitive details proportionate to what is needed for the service. Menus, allergies and arrival instructions help the chef do the job; unrelated personal information usually does not. Your myCHEF contact can help clarify how a privacy request affects the booking and which details need to be passed to the proposed professional.

sections.title: Give a trial or tasting a clear purpose
paragraphs: A trial is most useful when it resembles the work you want the chef to do. For household cooking, that might mean preparing a realistic family meal and a dish for later. For an occasion, a tasting may focus on selected menu items rather than reproducing the whole event. Explain what you want to assess before deciding the format.

Consider flavour, organisation, communication and how comfortably the food fits your preferences. An elaborate dish can be impressive without demonstrating the everyday cooking you need. Equally, a small tasting cannot show every aspect of service for a larger group, where staffing, equipment and timing introduce different demands.

Any cooking trial or tasting needs an agreed menu, location, duration and price. Ingredients, preparation and travel still involve work even for a small number of people. Afterwards, give clear feedback and discuss any changes before confirming a longer arrangement or final event menu. A successful trial is a useful decision point, not an automatic commitment.

sections.title: Help your chef understand the kitchen before arrival
paragraphs: A few practical details can make the first cooking day much smoother. Share the type of hob, oven capacity, available fridge space and any equipment the chef should know about. Photographs of the working area can help when the kitchen is unfamiliar. A small, well-organised kitchen can support excellent food when the menu is designed around it.

Discuss any specialist requirements before approving a dish. A menu that depends on several oven temperatures at once, a large freezer or equipment you do not own may need to be adapted. The aim is to choose food that can be cooked and served confidently in your actual home, within the agreed time.

Set aside preparation space and make essential utensils accessible. Let the chef know about delicate surfaces, appliances with unusual controls and items reserved for specific dietary needs. Confirm what cleanup includes as part of the booking, so the end of the visit is as well organised as the beginning.

sections.title: Make feedback specific enough to act on
paragraphs: The easiest way to improve an ongoing service is to describe the result you want. Instead of saying a meal was not right, explain whether it was too rich, too spicy, too large or served later than expected. A specific observation gives the chef a useful direction for the next menu and makes it easier to check whether the adjustment worked.

Tell us what you enjoyed as well. A dish you would happily eat again, a helpful way of organising the fridge or a cooking day that fitted your schedule can become part of the regular plan. Consistency is built from these details, not simply from repeating a menu without checking how it is being used.

For a service concern, contact myCHEF promptly with the relevant facts. The next step may be a menu change, a clearer brief, a revised schedule or discussion of a different available match. Any remedy depends on the circumstances and the booking terms; the starting point is a clear conversation.

cta.title: Let’s shape the details around you.
cta.body: Share your date or preferred cooking schedule, Dubai location and the number of people you are planning for. Tell us what you would most like help with, and we will discuss a suitable menu and service arrangement before confirming the details in writing.
